title: A barrier before the battle
q: How does intact skin contribute to innate defense against many pathogens?
options: It makes antibodies for every pathogen
why: Intact skin is a physical barrier that helps limit pathogen entry. It does not make infection impossible, and breaks or other routes can let pathogens enter.

recall.question: Which innate barrier helps block entry of many pathogens?
recall.why: Intact skin helps limit pathogen entry.

title: A cell engulfs a microbe
q: What process can a macrophage use to engulf an extracellular microbe?
why: A macrophage can engulf microbes by phagocytosis, enclosing material in a membrane-bound compartment for further processing.

recall.question: What is the process of a cell engulfing a microbe called?
recall.why: Phagocytosis encloses material inside a cell.

title: A rapid phagocyte
q: Which innate immune cell can engulf microbes and is abundant among circulating white blood cells?
why: Neutrophils are abundant phagocytic white blood cells that can engulf and digest microbes. The diagram omits their many other interactions.

recall.question: Can neutrophils engulf microbes?
options: Only if they are red blood cells
recall.why: Neutrophils are phagocytic white blood cells.

title: A fragment is displayed
q: An antigen-presenting cell displays a peptide on MHC class II. Which T-cell group can recognize that presentation through its receptor?
why: CD4 helper T cells can recognize peptides displayed by MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells. Full activation also requires additional signals.

recall.question: Which T-cell group recognizes peptide presented on MHC class II?
recall.why: CD4 T cells can recognize peptide–MHC II complexes.

title: An infected cell displays a clue
q: A nucleated cell displays a peptide on MHC class I. Which T-cell group can recognize that peptide–MHC complex?
why: CD8 cytotoxic T cells can recognize peptides presented on MHC class I. Recognition and activation involve additional molecular interactions.

recall.question: Which T-cell group recognizes peptide presented on MHC class I?
recall.why: CD8 T cells can recognize peptide–MHC I complexes.

title: A targeted cell is removed
q: After recognizing an appropriate infected target, what can a cytotoxic T cell induce in that target?
why: Activated cytotoxic T cells can induce apoptosis in appropriately recognized infected cells, limiting some intracellular infections.

recall.question: What can an activated cytotoxic T cell induce in an appropriately recognized target?
recall.why: Cytotoxic T cells can trigger programmed cell death in target cells.

title: A B cell changes jobs
q: After appropriate activation, which differentiated B-cell type secretes large amounts of antibody?
why: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies. Other descendants can become memory B cells.

recall.question: Which activated B-cell descendant secretes antibodies?

title: An antibody finds its target
q: What does the binding site of an antibody recognize?
why: An antibody binding site can recognize a compatible epitope, a particular part of an antigen. Binding depends on molecular fit and other interactions.

recall.question: What can an antibody binding site recognize?
recall.why: Antibody binding sites recognize compatible antigen epitopes.

title: Blocking a virus's attachment
q: An antibody binds a viral surface site needed for attachment to a host cell. What can this binding do?
why: An antibody that binds an appropriate viral surface site can neutralize by blocking attachment or entry. The effect depends on the antibody, virus and setting.

recall.question: What is one way an antibody can neutralize a virus?
options: Block its attachment to a host cell
recall.why: A suitable antibody can block viral attachment or entry.

title: A response can leave memory
q: After an adaptive response, which B-cell descendants can support a faster response to a later encounter with the same antigen?
why: Some activated B cells become memory cells that can contribute to a faster response upon a later encounter with the relevant antigen. Protection varies by context.

recall.question: Which B-cell descendant can support a faster later response to an antigen?
recall.why: Memory B cells can respond to a later encounter with the relevant antigen.

title: A helper signal
q: When a B cell receives the appropriate antigen and helper-T-cell signals, what can those signals help it do?
options: Turn into a red blood cell
why: Helper T-cell signals can support activation and proliferation of appropriately stimulated B cells. The diagram omits the required antigen recognition and other interactions.

recall.question: Which immune cell can helper T-cell signals support during an appropriate antibody response?
recall.why: Helper T-cell signals can support appropriately stimulated B cells.

title: A tag makes a target easier
q: Some complement proteins coat a microbe. What can that coating help phagocytes do?
why: Complement components can coat a microbe and enhance its recognition by phagocytes, a process called opsonization. Complement has other functions too.

recall.question: What is coating a microbe to improve phagocyte recognition called?
recall.why: Opsonization can help phagocytes recognize coated targets.

title: A warning between cells
q: A virus-infected cell releases interferons. What can those signals help neighboring cells do?
why: Interferons can signal neighboring cells to increase antiviral defenses. This response helps limit infection but does not guarantee complete protection.

recall.question: Which signal from an infected cell can help neighboring cells increase antiviral defenses?
recall.why: Interferons can trigger antiviral responses in neighboring cells.

title: A local alarm
q: In a local inflammatory response, histamine released by mast cells can affect nearby capillaries. Which effect can it promote?
options: Complete stopping of all blood flow
why: Histamine can promote dilation and increased permeability of nearby capillaries, helping immune cells and fluid reach the affected tissue.

recall.question: What can histamine promote in nearby capillaries during inflammation?
options: Permanent stopping of all blood flow
recall.why: Histamine can promote capillary dilation and increased permeability.

title: Preparing immune memory
q: A vaccine presents an antigen or instructions to make one. What adaptive response can this help establish?
options: A new species of red blood cell
why: Vaccination can prime antigen-specific adaptive immune responses and memory. The strength and duration of protection vary by vaccine, person and pathogen.

recall.question: What can vaccination help prime in adaptive immunity?
options: A new kind of red blood cell
recall.why: Vaccination can prime antigen-specific immune memory, with protection varying by context.
